raw_case_text: A 37-year-old female patient, who applied to the surgery clinic with complaints of abdominal pain, weakness, high fever, and chills. She had tenderness in the right upper quadrant and was in bad condition; leukocytes: 5500 UL, CRP: 140 mg/dl, GGT: 243 IU/L, ALP: 210 IU/L, tumor markers and echinococcal indirect hemagglutination (IHA) test results were negative. The patient was diagnosed with a "hydatid cyst" based on an eccentric abdominal CT done about a year earlier (Fig. 1), and she was treated with albendazole. Due to the location and size of the lesion, surgery was not possible. The histology of the surgical sample was unspecific, and the patient was medically followed up. Abdominal ultrasonography (US) depicted a multiloculated cystic lesion measuring 11x12x15 cm in size, with irregular thick walls and septations, dense content, occasionally leveling, and a tendency to merge with other lesions, was discovered in the liver segment IV-VIII. Under the guidance of US and CT, the Seldinger procedure was used to insert a 10F diameter percutaneous drainage catheter into the lesion, which was identified as an abscess (Fig. 2). A microscopic analysis of the drained purulent material indicated numerous leukocytes and Corynebacterium striatum in its culture. Clinical and laboratory results for the patient significantly improved within the first week of drainage. Despite the fluid flowing from the catheter seeming less purulent and being present in smaller amounts, the drainage continued. The internal septations showed notable thickening and contrast enhancement despite reduction in the lesion size. Similar results were observed with CT and the magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) examination, which was carried out to assess the link between the pancreas and the biliary system (Fig. 3). The abscess content of the lesion entirely vanished after about two months of percutaneous drainage therapy and periodic catheter modifications. Due to the patient's persistent yellowish catheter drainage and the lesion's persistent radiological appearance, particularly the contrast-enhancing internal thick septa, we hypothesized that our patient might have BCA-biliary cystadenocarcinoma (BCAC). Because the pre-operative diagnosis was BCAC and the clinical state was satisfactory, no culture was performed on the patient. The patient was then referred to a hepatobiliary surgery center. Despite having undergone two consecutive tru-cut biopsies of the lesion in this case, a histopathological diagnosis was not possible. The patient was not given Frozen. Laboratory results from the patient before surgery showed ALP=260 IU/L, ALT=722 IU/L, AST=838 IU/L, Albumin=27 g/dL, total bilirubin=1.74 mg/dL, direct bilirubin=0.85 mg/dL, GGT=639 IU/L, LDH=960 IU/L, and CRP=3.13 mg/L. Surgical intervention was performed with a Makuuchi J incision. A mass reaching approximately 20 cm in diameter in the central sector of the liver and compressing the left medial, caudate and right lobe was revealed with the help of intraoperative US. A previously placed drainage catheter area, located between segments 4-8, was observed. Central hepatectomy and isolated caudate lobectomy were performed six times with the help of Pringle maneuver, preserving the right posterior segments (Fig. 4). The lesion was reported histopathologically as BCA displaying high-grade dysplasia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old female presented with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, weakness, high fever, and chills.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had been diagnosed 1 year earlier at an outside facility with a central hepatic cyst on abdominal CT (presumed hydatid cyst) and treated medically with albendazole after an non-specific biopsy. She presented to the surgery clinic in poor general condition with acute right upper quadrant pain, weakness, high fever, and chills.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior diagnosis of central hepatic cyst 1 year earlier treated with oral albendazole.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right upper quadrant pain, weakness, high fever, and chills.

objective.physical_examination: Poor general condition with right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs showed WBC 5,500/uL, CRP 140 mg/dL, GGT 243 IU/L, ALP 210 IU/L, and negative tumor markers and Echinococcus indirect hemagglutination (IHA) serology. Preoperative labs prior to hepatectomy showed ALP 260 IU/L, ALT 722 IU/L, AST 838 IU/L, albumin 27 g/dL [2.7 g/dL], total bilirubin 1.74 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 0.85 mg/dL, GGT 639 IU/L, LDH 960 IU/L, and CRP 3.13 mg/L. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an 11 x 12 x 15 cm multiloculated cystic lesion with thick irregular walls and internal septations in hepatic segments IV-VIII.
objective.advanced_workup: US/CT-guided 10F percutaneous catheter drainage yielded purulent fluid with abundant leukocytes and positive culture for Corynebacterium striatum. Follow-up CT and MRCP after 2 months of drainage showed persistent contrast-enhancing thick internal septations despite abscess cavity collapse. Two consecutive tru-cut biopsies were non-diagnostic. Intraoperative ultrasound and central hepatectomy with isolated caudate lobectomy (via Makuuchi J-incision) resected a 20-cm central hepatic mass compressing the left medial, caudate, and right lobes; histopathology revealed biliary cystadenoma (BCA) with high-grade dysplasia.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Hepatic biliary cystadenoma (BCA) with high-grade dysplasia complicated by secondary Corynebacterium striatum abscess (initially misdiagnosed as a hepatic hydatid cyst, which was excluded by negative Echinococcus IHA and final surgical histopathology). After 2 months of percutaneous catheter drainage to resolve the superinfected abscess, the patient underwent central hepatectomy and isolated caudate lobectomy.
